title: Capacity Planning
description: Estimate traffic, size infrastructure, and plan for growth. Learn how to calculate throughput, apply headroom, and choose the right resources to avoid costly overprovisioning or dangerous underprovisioning.

data.text: Capacity planning answers one question: does the system have enough resources to handle its expected load? For senior engineers, this is not guesswork. It is a calculation based on user data, traffic patterns, and growth projections.
Bad capacity planning leads to two failure modes. Overprovisioning wastes money. Underprovisioning causes outages, slow responses, and lost revenue. The goal is to find the sweet spot.
Start with the number of users and their behavior. A system with 100,000 daily active users does not need the same capacity as a system where each user sends 50 requests per minute.

data.title: Steps to Estimate Traffic
items: Calculate daily active users (DAU) or monthly active users (MAU)
Estimate average requests per user per day
Multiply DAU by requests to get daily total requests
Divide by 86,400 seconds to get requests per second (RPS)
Multiply by a peak multiplier (usually 2x to 5x) to account for spikes

data.title: Traffic Estimation Example
data.content: If your app has 50,000 daily active users and each user makes an average of 20 requests per day:
data.code:
Daily requests = 50,000 users × 20 requests = 1,000,000 requests
Daily RPS = 1,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 11.6 RPS
Peak RPS (3x multiplier) = 11.6 × 3 ≈ 35 RPS

data.text: Headroom is the buffer between your current load and your maximum capacity. Most teams plan for 2x to 3x headroom above peak expected load. This absorbs unexpected spikes without requiring an emergency scaling action.

Once you know your target RPS, you can size your servers. A rule of thumb is that a modern application server handles 500 to 2,000 RPS for typical business logic. Databases, especially relational ones, handle fewer concurrent writes. Add caching to reduce database load.

data.caption: Capacity planning flow from traffic estimation to resource sizing
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Estimate DAU/MAU] --> B[Calculate daily requests]
    B --> C[Derive peak RPS]
    C --> D[Apply headroom multiplier]
    D --> E[Size application servers]
    E --> F[Size database cluster]
    F --> G[Add caching layer]
    G --> H[Validate with load test]

data.title: Key Principle
data.text: Always validate capacity plans with a load test before launch. Simulated traffic often reveals bottlenecks that calculations miss, such as connection pool exhaustion or slow database queries under concurrency.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Calculate peak RPS from DAU, requests per user, and a spike multiplier
Plan for 2x to 3x headroom above peak load
Size servers based on RPS targets, not just user counts
Validate capacity plans with load testing before launch
Revisit capacity plans quarterly or after major feature launches
data.takeaway: Capacity planning turns guesswork into a repeatable calculation. Measure, model, and verify.

items.question: What if I do not have accurate user data?
items.answer: Use industry benchmarks for your domain. E-commerce sites average 20 to 40 requests per user per day. Content sites average 5 to 15. Start with a range and refine after launch.

items.question: Should I size for future growth?
items.answer: Yes, but cautiously. Plan for 6 to 12 months of organic growth. Planning for years ahead often leads to overprovisioning and wasted spend.

items.question: What tools help with capacity planning?
items.answer: Load testing tools (k6, Gatling), monitoring platforms (Datadog, New Relic), and cloud cost calculators all help. Combine them with spreadsheet models for the most accurate estimates.

data.title: Capacity Plan for a Fitness App
data.description: Your company is launching a fitness tracking app. Research shows 25,000 users will sign up in the first month. Each user will send an average of 15 requests per day, with expected 4x spikes during morning hours. Create a capacity plan covering RPS, server count, and database sizing.
data.expectedOutcome: A written capacity plan with peak RPS calculations, headroom assumptions, and a recommendation for application server and database sizing.
